profile.feeling: Warm, sharp and medicinal: ginger tea for a cold — and a word with Qurʾānic resonance.

senses.def: ginger — the rhizome, fresh or dried and ground (mass noun)

examples.tr: I drink tea with ginger in winter.

examples.text: قَشِّرْ قِطْعَةً مِنَ الزَّنْجَبِيلِ الطَّازَجِ وَقَطِّعْهَا.
examples.tr: Peel a piece of fresh ginger and chop it.
Ginger helps to relieve nausea.

phrases.text: وَيُسْقَوْنَ فِيهَا كَأْسًا كَانَ مِزَاجُهَا زَنْجَبِيلًا
phrases.tr: And they will be given to drink there a cup whose mixture is ginger.
phrases.meaning: Ginger as a flavour of the drinks of Paradise — the word is in the Qurʾān.

synonyms.nuance: Egyptian Arabic pronunciation ganzabīl, with the consonants swapped (Wiktionary)
Moroccan Arabic form skanjbīr (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: From Classical Syriac ܙܢܓܒܝܠ (zangabīl), from Sauraseni Prakrit siṃgivera, from Old Tamil iñcivēr (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Arabic زَنْجَبِيل, Hebrew זַנְגְּבִיל (zangvil), Turkish zencefil, Ancient Greek ζιγγίβερις and Latin zingiber (→ English ginger, German Ingwer) all go back to the same South Indian word.
pitfalls: In Egypt the consonants are often swapped: جنزبيل (ganzabīl, Wiktionary) — write زَنْجَبِيل.
Masculine: زَنْجَبِيلٌ طَازَجٌ (fresh ginger), not *طَازَجَةٌ.
subtleties: A mass noun: a piece is قِطْعَةُ زَنْجَبِيلٍ, the root جِذْرُ الزَّنْجَبِيلِ; there is no unit noun.

profile.feeling: Aniseed aroma: crisp Mediterranean salads and digestive teas.

senses.def: fennel — the plant, its bulb and stalks eaten as a vegetable, and its seeds as a spice
dill (in older texts; Wiktionary)

examples.tr: I cut the fennel into thin slices for the salad.
Fennel-seed tea soothes the stomach.

examples.text: يَنْمُو الشَّمَرُ الْبَرِّيُّ عَلَى جَوَانِبِ الطُّرُقِ.
examples.tr: Wild fennel grows along the roadsides.

examples.text: فِي بَعْضِ الْكُتُبِ الْقَدِيمَةِ يَعْنِي الشَّمَرُ نَبَاتَ الشِّبِتِّ.
examples.tr: In some old books šamar means dill.

synonyms.nuance: the classical and old-medical word, from Middle Persian; Wiktionary also gives it for dill
the word in North Africa (Wiktionary: Moroccan Arabic, and fennel in al-Andalus); in the Najd it names other plants

etymology.text: From Aramaic (Classical Syriac šammārā, šummārā, “fennel”), ultimately from Akkadian šimru; also found in Hebrew שֻׁמָּר (šummār, “fennel”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Hebrew שׁוּמָר (shumar, fennel) is the same Akkadian-Aramaic word.
The Greek town of Marathon is named after fennel (μάραθο): the battlefield was a “fennel field”.
pitfalls: Without vowels شمر is also the verb شَمَّرَ (to tuck up): شَمَّرَ عَنْ سَاعِدَيْهِ = he rolled up his sleeves (got down to work).
Wiktionary tags شَمَر “rare” in its classical senses; it is the everyday word in Egypt (Wiktionary’s Egyptian Arabic translation).
subtleties: One word for the vegetable and the spice: the seeds are بُذُورُ الشَّمَرِ; context tells which is meant.

profile.feeling: An elegant, rather expensive spring vegetable — restaurant food more than home cooking.

senses.def: asparagus — the plant and its edible spears (mass noun)

examples.text: شَوَيْتُ الْهِلْيَوْنَ مَعَ قَلِيلٍ مِنْ زَيْتِ الزَّيْتُونِ.
examples.tr: I grilled the asparagus with a little olive oil.
Asparagus is expensive this season.
I ordered asparagus soup at the restaurant.

synonyms.nuance: the same word pronounced hilyūn (Wiktionary lists both)
Egyptian Arabic loan from European asparagus (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: From Classical Syriac helyōn, from Ancient Greek ἕλειον (héleion, “asparagus”), the neuter of ἕλειος (“of the marshland”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: A Greek word in Arabic dress: هِلْيَوْن is ἕλειον, “the marsh plant”.
In Egypt people also use the European loan اسبراجوس (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: Three vocalizations are in use — هِلْيَوْن, هِلْيُون, هَلْيُون (Wiktionary); this course uses هِلْيَوْن, and you will often hear hilyūn.
أَخْضَر and أَبْيَض are diptotes: هِلْيَوْنٌ أَخْضَرُ (green asparagus), with no tanwīn on the adjective.
subtleties: A masculine mass noun: الْهِلْيَوْنُ الطَّازَجُ (fresh asparagus).

profile.feeling: Egyptian winter comfort food: taro cooked in a green sauce of chard and coriander — and the dish of the Coptic Epiphany.

senses.def: taro (collective; one corm = قُلْقَاسَة)
cardoon or artichoke (obsolete, Wiktionary)

examples.text: يَطْبُخُ الْمِصْرِيُّونَ الْقُلْقَاسَ مَعَ السِّلْقِ وَالْكُزْبَرَةِ.
examples.tr: Egyptians cook taro with chard and coriander.
Peel the taro and cut it into cubes.

examples.text: يَأْكُلُ الْأَقْبَاطُ الْقُلْقَاسَ فِي عِيدِ الْغِطَاسِ.
examples.tr: Copts eat taro at the feast of the Epiphany.
I bought a big taro.

examples.text: فِي كُتُبِ النَّبَاتِ الْقَدِيمَةِ قَدْ يَعْنِي الْقُلْقَاسُ الْخُرْشُوفَ.
examples.tr: In old botanical books qulqās can mean the artichoke.

examples.text: لَا يُسْتَعْمَلُ الْقُلْقَاسُ الْيَوْمَ بِمَعْنَى الْخُرْشُوفِ.
examples.tr: Today qulqās is no longer used in the sense of artichoke.

synonyms.nuance: Moroccan Arabic name, literally “reed potato” (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: From Classical Syriac qōlqās, qalqā (“taro”), said to be from Egyptian; Ancient Greek κολοκασία (kolokasía) first meant the sacred lotus and only later taro (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Arabic قُلْقَاس and Greek κολοκάσι (taro in Cyprus) are one word that travelled between Egypt, Aramaic and Greek.
pitfalls: Raw taro irritates mouth and skin; it is always cooked, and many cooks wear gloves to peel it.
In Cairo the q is a glottal stop: ʔulʔās. Wiktionary also lists the spellings قُلْقَاص and قُرْقَاص.
subtleties: Collective: الْقُلْقَاسُ (taro as food), قُلْقَاسَة (one corm), قُلْقَاسَات (corms counted).

profile.feeling: Bitter spring greens and herbal remedies; yellow flowers in the fields.

senses.def: dandelion (Taraxacum) — the plant and its leaves eaten as bitter greens
common chicory, Belgian endive (Wiktionary)

examples.tr: Dandelion is used in folk medicine.

examples.text: أَوْرَاقُ الطَّرْخَشْقُونِ الصَّغِيرَةُ لَذِيذَةٌ فِي السَّلَطَةِ.
examples.tr: Young dandelion leaves are tasty in salad.

examples.text: تَظْهَرُ أَزْهَارُ الطَّرْخَشْقُونِ الصَّفْرَاءُ فِي الرَّبِيعِ.
examples.tr: The yellow dandelion flowers appear in spring.

examples.text: يُطْلَقُ الطَّرْخَشْقُونُ أَيْضًا عَلَى الْهِنْدِبَاءِ الْبَرِّيَّةِ.
examples.tr: ṭaraḫšaqūn is also used for wild chicory.

examples.text: فِي الطِّبِّ الْقَدِيمِ كَانَ الطَّرْخَشْقُونُ اسْمًا لِلْهِنْدِبَاءِ أَيْضًا.
examples.tr: In old medicine ṭaraḫšaqūn was also a name for chicory.

synonyms.nuance: the general word for chicory-like greens; Wiktionary also gives it for dandelion
old name, literally “bitter” (Wiktionary marks it obsolete)

etymology.text: From Middle Persian *tarrag-ī škōhān, literally “herb of the poor”, so called because it was rarely eaten except in times of famine (Wiktionary).

funFacts: English and German name the leaf after a lion’s tooth (dent-de-lion, Löwenzahn); the Persian name inside Arabic speaks of poverty — “the poor man’s herb”.
The botanists’ Latin Taraxacum is usually traced to this Arabic-Persian word.
pitfalls: Wiktionary lists many spellings: طَرْخَشْقُون, طَرَخْشَقُون, طَرَخَشْقُون, and forms with طَلْـ such as طَلْخَشْقُون.
In everyday speech many people simply say هِنْدِبَاء for both dandelion and chicory.
subtleties: A learned word: in markets the bitter wild greens are sold under the name هِنْدِبَاء (Levantine هندبة), not طَرْخَشْقُون.

profile.feeling: Pink pickled turnips next to falafel and shawarma.

senses.def: turnip (Brassica rapa; mass noun)
similar brassicas: kale, rape, rutabaga (Wiktionary)

examples.tr: I like pickled turnips with falafel.
They colour the turnip pickle with beetroot.
The farmer planted turnips in autumn.

synonyms.nuance: Persian loan for turnip (also rutabaga; and “parabola” in mathematics) (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: From the root ل ف ت (“to twist, to pull out of the ground”); ultimately from Proto-Semitic *lapt-, compare Hebrew לֶפֶת (lefet), Classical Syriac laftā and Akkadian laptu (“turnip”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Hebrew לֶפֶת and Arabic لِفْت are the same Semitic word — Akkadian farmers already said laptu.
Its synonym شَلْجَم comes from Persian šalġam, ultimately from Greek σικελικόν “the Sicilian one” — the same source as سِلْق (chard) (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: Same letters as the verb لَفَتَ (lafata, to turn, to attract): لَفَتَ انْتِبَاهِي = it caught my attention.
Vowel: lift with i in MSA; Moroccan Arabic says laft (Wiktionary).
subtleties: A mass noun in Wiktionary: one turnip is حَبَّةُ لِفْتٍ.
The Levantine pink pickle owes its colour to a slice of beetroot in the jar.

profile.feeling: Bitter, “cleansing” greens: Levantine hindbeh fried with onions, and chicory “coffee”.

senses.def: chicory (Cichorium intybus), including the pale Belgian endive (witloof) and the wild leaves cooked as greens
endive (Cichorium endivia): curly endive, frisée, escarole
dandelion (Wiktionary)

examples.text: الْهِنْدِبَاءُ الْمَطْبُوخَةُ بِالزَّيْتِ وَالْبَصَلِ طَبَقٌ لُبْنَانِيٌّ مَعْرُوفٌ.
examples.tr: Chicory greens cooked with oil and onion are a well-known Lebanese dish.

examples.text: يُحَمَّصُ جِذْرُ الْهِنْدِبَاءِ وَيُشْرَبُ بَدَلَ الْقَهْوَةِ.
examples.tr: Chicory root is roasted and drunk instead of coffee.
Chicory tastes a little bitter.

examples.text: أَضَفْتُ أَوْرَاقَ الْهِنْدِبَاءِ الْمُجَعَّدَةَ إِلَى السَّلَطَةِ.
examples.tr: I added curly endive leaves to the salad.
I bought (some) endive for the salad.

examples.text: تَنْبُتُ الْهِنْدِبَاءُ الْبَرِّيَّةُ ذَاتُ الزَّهْرِ الْأَصْفَرِ فِي الْحُقُولِ.
examples.tr: Wild hindibāʾ with yellow flowers — the dandelion — grows in the fields.
Some people call the dandelion hindibāʾ.

synonyms.nuance: Levantine everyday form (hindbe) for the cooked bitter greens
Moroccan Arabic word for endive, from European chicorée (Wiktionary)
spelling without the final hamza (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: From Aramaic hendǝḇā, cognate with Arabic هَدَب (“twisted leaves or sprigs”). From Semitic also Byzantine Greek ἔντυβον, whence Late Latin intibus and English endive (Wiktionary).

funFacts: English endive (and its cousins in the European languages) goes back, through Greek and Latin, to this Semitic word.
pitfalls: Diptote: no tanwīn — هِنْدِبَاءُ, accusative and genitive هِنْدِبَاءَ (Wiktionary).
One word for chicory, endive and (loosely) dandelion: Arabic does not split them — add a description if you need precision.
subtleties: Feminine: الْهِنْدِبَاءُ الْمُرَّةُ (the bitter chicory); Wiktionary treats it as a collective without a unit noun.

senses.def: purslane (Portulaca oleracea), eaten raw or cooked (mass noun)

examples.text: تَطْبُخُ أُمِّي الرِّجْلَةَ مَعَ الْأَرُزِّ وَالطَّمَاطِمِ.
examples.tr: My mother cooks purslane with rice and tomatoes.

examples.text: تَنْبُتُ الرِّجْلَةُ وَحْدَهَا فِي الْحُقُولِ فِي الصَّيْفِ.
examples.tr: Purslane comes up by itself in the fields in summer.
I bought fresh purslane for the salad.

phrases.meaning: utterly foolish — purslane grows where the flood will sweep it away

synonyms.nuance: the everyday Levantine name (properly “a herb, a green”); it is the purslane in fattoush
from Aramaic parpəḥīnā; Wiktionary’s main entry for purslane
the classical name, “the foolish herb”

etymology.text: Alternative form of رِجْل (rijl, “purslane”), which Wiktionary files under the same Proto-Semitic *rigl- as رِجْل “foot, leg”.

funFacts: The classical name is الْبَقْلَةُ الْحَمْقَاءُ, “the foolish herb” — it grows in the beds of seasonal streams, where floods wash it away.
Greeks eat the same weed in salads as γλιστρίδα.
pitfalls: Without vowels رجلة can also be رُجْلَة (rujla, manhood) — Wiktionary lists both.
The name changes by region: رِجْلَة (e.g. Egypt), بَقْلَة (Levant); in literature also فَرْفَحِين and الْبَقْلَةُ الْحَمْقَاءُ.
subtleties: Feminine and uncounted: الرِّجْلَةُ طَازَجَةٌ (the purslane is fresh).

Nettles are cooked like spinach.
Put on gloves before picking nettles.

synonyms.nuance: another dictionary name, feminine (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: From the root ق ر ص, whose verb قَرَصَ means “to pinch; to bite, to sting” (Wiktionary) — “the stinging one”, on the plant-name pattern fuʿʿāl.

funFacts: German Brennnessel is the “burning” nettle; Arabic قُرَّاص is the “pinching” one — both languages name the sting.
pitfalls: قُرْص (qurṣ), with one r, is a disc or a tablet: قُرْصُ دَوَاءٍ (a pill) — same letters without vowels.
subtleties: A masculine mass noun: الْقُرَّاصُ يَلْسَعُ (nettles sting).

profile.feeling: Garlicky green leaves of European spring woods; in Arabic simply “wild garlic”.

senses.def: wild garlic, ramsons (Allium ursinum) — literally “wild garlic”; also any garlic gathered wild

examples.tr: We picked wild garlic in the forest.

examples.text: أَوْرَاقُ الثُّومِ الْبَرِّيِّ تُؤْكَلُ نَيِّئَةً أَوْ مَطْبُوخَةً.
examples.tr: Wild garlic leaves are eaten raw or cooked.

examples.text: صَنَعَتْ صَلْصَةً خَضْرَاءَ مِنَ الثُّومِ الْبَرِّيِّ.
examples.tr: She made a green sauce from wild garlic.

profile.synonymsNone: No established single word: ramsons is not part of traditional Arab cooking, so it is described as “wild garlic”.

etymology.text: ثُوم “garlic”, inherited from Proto-Semitic *ṯūm- (cognate with Hebrew שׁוּם shum) + بَرِّيّ “wild”, the nisba of بَرّ “land, open country” (Wiktionary).
etymology.src: Wiktionary (kaikki.org): ثوم; the phrase has no entry

funFacts: German Bärlauch and Latin Allium ursinum say “bear’s garlic”; Arabic, like English, just says “wild garlic”.
pitfalls: بَرِّيّ (barrī, wild) and بَرِيء (barīʾ, innocent) sound alike — listen for the doubled r and the final hamza.
subtleties: Two words, one noun: the adjective follows the noun in case and definiteness — الثُّومُ الْبَرِّيُّ, الثُّومَ الْبَرِّيَّ, الثُّومِ الْبَرِّيِّ.

profile.feeling: A pale, sweet winter root — at home in European kitchens, a newcomer in Arab ones.

senses.def: parsnip — literally “white carrot” (collective; one parsnip = جَزَرَةٌ بَيْضَاءُ)

examples.tr: I roasted the parsnips in the oven.
Parsnips taste sweet.
I bought one parsnip.

profile.synonymsNone: No other name in common use; Wiktionary gives only جَزَر أَبْيَض.

etymology.text: جَزَر “carrot”, from Persian گزر (gazar) + أَبْيَض “white”; Wiktionary gives جَزَر أَبْيَض as the translation of parsnip.
etymology.src: Wiktionary (kaikki.org): جزر and the translation table of English parsnip

funFacts: Botanically the description fits: parsnip and carrot belong to the same family, the Apiaceae.
pitfalls: Genuinely white carrots also exist, and جَزَرٌ أَبْيَضُ can mean them too — a picture or the context decides.
Agreement changes with the unit noun: جَزَرٌ أَبْيَضُ (parsnips), but جَزَرَةٌ بَيْضَاءُ (one parsnip); both adjectives are diptotes.
subtleties: Counted parsnips: جَزَرَاتٌ بَيْضَاءُ — a non-human plural takes a feminine singular adjective.

profile.feeling: Sour, lemony leaves — a wild spring green.

senses.def: sorrel (Rumex), whose leaves are eaten for their sour taste
acidosis (medicine; Wiktionary)

examples.tr: Sorrel leaves have a sour taste.
We gathered wild sorrel in spring.

examples.text: أُضِيفُ قَلِيلًا مِنَ الْحُمَّاضِ إِلَى الْحَسَاءِ.
examples.tr: I add a little sorrel to the soup.
The patient developed ketoacidosis.

synonyms.nuance: “garden sorrel”, the cultivated plant (Wiktionary’s translation of sorrel)

etymology.text: From the root ح م ض (“sour”), like حَامِض (“sour”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The root ḥ-m-ḍ “sour” matches Hebrew ח-מ-ץ: חָמוּץ (ḥamuts, sour) and חָמֵץ (ḥamets, leavened food).
pitfalls: In medicine حُمَّاض means acidosis (Wiktionary) — context decides.
حُمَّاض (sorrel) and حَامِض (sour) share the root but are different words.
subtleties: The pattern fuʿʿāl often names plants by a quality: حُمَّاض “the sour one”, قُرَّاص “the stinging one”.

etymology.text: فُجْل “radish”, from Aramaic puḡlā, from Akkadian puglu + حَارّ “hot, pungent”; Wiktionary gives فُجْل حَارّ as the translation of horseradish.
etymology.src: Wiktionary (kaikki.org): فجل and the translation table of English horseradish

funFacts: Japanese wasabi is a close relative, and cheap “wasabi” paste is often coloured horseradish.
pitfalls: In a salad, فُجْلٌ حَارٌّ can simply mean a sharp-tasting radish — context decides.
Both words take the article: الْفُجْلُ الْحَارُّ, not *الْفُجْلُ حَارٌّ (that would be a sentence: “the radish is hot”).
subtleties: حَارّ means both “hot” in temperature and “hot, spicy”; here it is the sting of mustard oil.

examples.text: كَانَتِ الْقُرَّةُ عِنْدَ الْقُدَمَاءِ دَوَاءً يُهَدِّئُ الْتِهَابَ الْعَيْنِ.
examples.tr: For the ancients, qurra was a remedy that soothed an inflamed eye.

phrases.meaning: a delight, a source of joy (often a beloved child)

synonyms.nuance: cress in general — garden cress, bitter-cress and watercress (Wiktionary)
properly rocket (arugula); Wiktionary lists watercress as its second sense

etymology.text: Wiktionary gives قُرَّة the senses “any means to soothe inflamed eyes”, “watercress” and “water-parsnip”; the word belongs to the root ق ر ر (“to be cool, to settle”).

funFacts: The same word is in the idiom قُرَّةُ عَيْنٍ, “coolness of the eye” = a delight: Pharaoh’s wife calls the baby Moses قُرَّتُ عَيْنٍ لِي وَلَكَ (Qurʾān 28:9).
pitfalls: Without vowels قرة can also be قِرَّة (qirra, coldness) — Wiktionary lists both.
Watercress and rocket (جِرْجِير) are easily confused in markets and translations; Wiktionary even lists “watercress” as a second sense of جِرْجِير.
subtleties: Feminine mass noun: الْقُرَّةُ طَازَجَةٌ (the watercress is fresh).

synonyms.nuance: classical name of cress (Lepidium sativum and other cresses) (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: Verbal noun of رَشِدَ (rašida, “to be rightly guided”); the plant name has the same form (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Same root as رُشْد (maturity, sound mind): سِنُّ الرُّشْدِ = the age of majority.
pitfalls: رَشَاد the plant, رَشَاد “right guidance” and the man’s name رَشَاد (Rashad) are one word — context decides.
subtleties: Most people know the seeds, حَبُّ الرَّشَادِ, sold by the herbalist (عَطَّار), better than the leaves.

etymology.text: From Classical Syriac silqā, from Aramaic, ultimately from Ancient Greek σικελικόν (sikelikón, “the Sicilian one”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Chard is “the Sicilian vegetable”: Greek σικελικόν gave Arabic سِلْق — and, through Persian, شَلْجَم (turnip).
Hebrew סֶלֶק (selek) is the same Aramaic word — but in Hebrew it means beetroot.
pitfalls: Same letters as سَلْق (salq, boiling) and the verb سَلَقَ (to boil): بَيْضٌ مَسْلُوقٌ = boiled eggs.
Not شَمَنْدَر (beetroot), although both are the same species.
subtleties: Botanically chard and beetroot are one species (Beta vulgaris): سِلْق is grown for its leaves, شَمَنْدَر for its root.

etymology.text: Borrowed from Aramaic gargīrā (“rocket”), from Akkadian girgirû (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Modern Hebrew גַּרְגִּיר (gargir) is the same plant and the same Aramaic word.
With Egyptian g, gargīr sounds almost exactly like the Aramaic original.
pitfalls: Vocalized جِرْجِير (jirjīr) in Wiktionary’s entry and جَرْجِير (jarjīr) in its translation tables; Egyptians say gargīr.
Not قُرَّة (watercress), although Wiktionary lists watercress as a second sense of جِرْجِير.
subtleties: A masculine mass noun: الْجِرْجِيرُ طَازَجٌ (the rocket is fresh).

profile.feeling: Green, slippery and garlicky — the soul food of Egypt, eaten with rice or bread and chicken or rabbit.

senses.def: jute mallow, molokhia — the leaves of Corchorus olitorius and the dish made of them
okra (Moroccan Arabic; Wiktionary)

examples.tr: We eat molokhia with rice and chicken.

examples.text: أَضِيفِي الثُّومَ الْمَقْلِيَّ إِلَى الْمُلُوخِيَّةِ فِي النِّهَايَةِ.
examples.tr: Add (f.) the fried garlic to the molokhia at the end.

examples.text: فِي تُونِسَ تُطْبَخُ الْمُلُوخِيَّةُ مِنْ أَوْرَاقٍ مُجَفَّفَةٍ مَطْحُونَةٍ.
examples.tr: In Tunisia molokhia is cooked from dried, ground leaves.
In Morocco, “mulūḫiyya” means okra.

examples.text: طَلَبْتُ مُلُوخِيَّةً فِي مَطْعَمٍ بِفَاسَ فَجَاءَتْنِي بَامِيَةٌ.
examples.tr: I ordered mulūḫiyya in a restaurant in Fez and was brought okra.

synonyms.nuance: spelling variant with final alif (Wiktionary)

funFacts: The Fatimid caliph al-Ḥākim bi-Amr Allāh banned mulūḫiyya in Egypt in the early 11th century.
Egyptian cooks traditionally gasp (شَهْقَة) as they pour the sizzling garlic into the pot — kitchen lore for a good result.
Greek μολόχα (molócha, mallow) is its cousin: the name came into Arabic from Greek.
pitfalls: In Morocco مْلُوخِيَّة means okra, not jute mallow (Wiktionary).
Spelled with šadda: ـيَّة (mulūḫiyya); Wiktionary also lists مُلُوخِيَّا, مُلُوكِيَّة and مُلُوكِيَّا.
subtleties: One word for the plant and the dish. In Egypt the leaves are minced into a slippery soup; in the Levant they are often cooked whole.
Popular etymology links the name to مُلُوك “kings” (a “royal” dish); Wiktionary derives it from Greek.

Red onion is sweeter than white.
I bought a big red onion.

synonyms.nuance: “purple onion”, a rarer description (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: بَصَل “onion”, a common Semitic word (compare Hebrew בָּצָל) + أَحْمَر “red”; Wiktionary gives بَصَل أَحْمَر as the translation of red onion.
etymology.src: Wiktionary (kaikki.org): بصل and the translation table of English red onion

funFacts: Arabic, English and German (rote Zwiebel) all call it “red”, though the colour is really purple.
pitfalls: أَحْمَر is a diptote with the feminine حَمْرَاء: بَصَلٌ أَحْمَرُ, but بَصَلَةٌ حَمْرَاءُ (one red onion) — never *بَصَلَةٌ أَحْمَرُ.
subtleties: Counted red onions: بَصَلَاتٌ حَمْرَاءُ — a non-human plural takes a feminine singular adjective.
